questions.enonce_markdown:
**2.** (a) State the Logical relationship between the following sets of propositions:

(i) All bananas are sweet fruits and No bananas are non-sweet fruits

(ii) Some Europeans are black persons and some Europeans are not black persons

(iii) All Logic exercises are exciting exercises and all non-exciting exercises are non-logic exercises

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Equivalence (2 marks).** "All bananas are sweet fruits" is an A proposition (All B are S). "No bananas are non-sweet fruits" is an E proposition (No B are non-S). The second is the **obverse** of the first (change the quality, replace the predicate by its complement). A proposition and its obverse are **logically equivalent**: they always have the same truth value (both true or both false) and each follows from the other.

**(ii) Sub-contraries (2 marks).** "Some Europeans are black persons" is an I proposition and "Some Europeans are not black persons" is an O proposition, with the same subject and predicate. I and O are **sub-contraries**: they **cannot both be false**, but they **can both be true** (as here). If one is false, the other must be true; if one is true, the other is undetermined. (This is the traditional square of opposition, which assumes that the subject term is not empty.)

**(iii) Equivalence by contraposition (2 marks).** "All Logic exercises are exciting exercises" is an A proposition (All L are E). "All non-exciting exercises are non-logic exercises" is the A proposition (All non-E are non-L), its **contrapositive** (the terms exchanged and replaced by their complements). An A proposition and its contrapositive are **logically equivalent**: they have the same truth value.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Using the terms: "Valid arguments" as the middle term, "sound arguments" as the major term and "weak arguments" as minor term

(i) Construct an AEE-2 argument. (3 marks)

(ii) Give out the inverse of the major premise of the syllogism in a(i) above. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) An AEE-2 syllogism (3 marks).** The code AEE-2 means: major premise A, minor premise E, conclusion E, in the **second figure** (the middle term is the predicate of both premises). With $P$ = sound arguments (major term), $M$ = valid arguments (middle term), $S$ = weak arguments (minor term):

- Major premise (A, $P$ - $M$): **All sound arguments are valid arguments.**
- Minor premise (E, $S$ - $M$): **No weak arguments are valid arguments.**
- Conclusion (E, $S$ - $P$): **Therefore, no weak arguments are sound arguments.**

Checks: the middle term "valid arguments" is the predicate of both premises (second figure) and is distributed in the E premise; the major term "sound arguments" is distributed in the premise (subject of an A) as in the conclusion (predicate of an E); one premise is negative and so is the conclusion. The syllogism is valid (it is the mood traditionally called Camestres).

**(ii) The inverse of the major premise (4 marks).** The major premise is "All sound arguments are valid arguments" (All $P$ are $M$). The inverse of an A proposition "All $S$ are $P$" is the O proposition "Some non-$S$ are not $P$" (equivalently the I proposition "Some non-$S$ are non-$P$"). It is obtained in these steps:

1. Contrapositive: All non-valid arguments are non-sound arguments.
2. Subalternation (A to I): Some non-valid arguments are non-sound arguments.
3. Simple conversion: Some non-sound arguments are non-valid arguments.
4. Obversion: Some non-sound arguments are not valid arguments.

**The inverse is therefore: "Some non-sound (unsound) arguments are not valid arguments"** (equivalently: "Some non-sound arguments are non-valid arguments"), an O proposition.

Warning: the tempting answer "All non-sound arguments are non-valid arguments" is **not** a valid inverse (it is the fallacy of denying the antecedent: unsound arguments can be valid, for instance when a premise is false). The inference to the particular proposition rests on the assumption that invalid arguments exist, which is true.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Using the symbols in parenthesis, translate the following ordinary language statements into symbolic form:

(i) Either Beatrice is beautiful (p) and intelligent (q) or she is ugly (r) and dull (s)

(ii) If airports are secured places (A) then luggage are safe (L) but if airports are not secured places, then theft is possible (T)

(iii) A child is dependent (C) if and only if s/he still lives with the parents (P) and is being sponsored by the parents (S)

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2 marks).** "Either ... or ..." joins two conjunctions: $(p \cdot q) \vee (r \cdot s)$.

**(ii) (2 marks).** "But" is a conjunction of two conditionals: if $A$ then $L$, and if not-$A$ then $T$:

$$(A \supset L) \cdot (\sim A \supset T)$$

**(iii) (2 marks).** "If and only if" is the biconditional; its right-hand side is the conjunction of the two conditions ("lives with the parents **and** is being sponsored"):

$$C \equiv (P \cdot S)$$

(The brackets matter: $C \equiv P \cdot S$ without brackets would be ambiguous.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Use the truth-table to determine which statement is Tautologous, Contingent or Contradictory:

(i) $(p \vee q) \supset (q \cdot p)$

(ii) $(p \cdot q) \equiv (q \cdot p)$

(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) $(p \vee q) \supset (q \cdot p)$ (3 marks).**

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \vee q$ | $q \cdot p$ | $(p \vee q) \supset (q \cdot p)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | F |
| F | F | F | F | T |

The final column contains both T and F, so the statement is **contingent**.

**(ii) $(p \cdot q) \equiv (q \cdot p)$ (3 marks).**

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \cdot q$ | $q \cdot p$ | $(p \cdot q) \equiv (q \cdot p)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T |
| F | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | F | F | T |

The final column is true in every row, so the statement is a **tautology** (it expresses the commutation of conjunction).
